articles.title: China’s factories are back in growth
articles.summary: Beijing: China's factory activity returned to growth in September, an official survey showed on Wednesday, as easing weather disruptions allowed factories to resume operations and a global artificial intelligence boom supported the industrial sector.The official manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) rose to 50.1 from 49.8 in August, ending two straight months of contraction, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. That matched the median forecast of 50.1 in a Reuters poll.Also Read: China's manufacturing scale shows the path to first-world statusThe 50-point mark separates expansion from contraction.The sub-index for new orders was at 50.5 while the sub-index for production was at 51.7, the data showed.The reading is broadly in line with a private survey by RatingDog, which showed manufacturing PMI at 52.1 in September.A run of soft economic readings has heightened pressure on policymakers to roll out further support measures, as retail sales and investment remain weak.China unveiled measures on Tuesday designed to steer cheaper credit into a range of sectors including infrastructure and technology, as well as expanding support for home buyers.While these issues have featured in previous policy statements, a fresh round of support could help shore up the economy's weakest areas, said Lynn Song, ING's chief economist for Greater China.Also Read: China's factory output growth quickens in August, retail sales slowThe non-manufacturing PMI, which covers services and construction, came in at 50.2 in September, compared with August's 49.0, according to the NBS.China has relied heavily on exports and industrial production to support growth this year, as weak domestic demand and a prolonged property downturn have weighed on household and business confidence.The country's global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year.But geopolitical uncertainty and growing trade frictions pose risks to the export outlook, as Chinese goods ranging from high-end electronics to household products face greater scrutiny in overseas markets.China and the United States on Monday said they will pursue tariff cuts on $60 billion worth of goods imported from each other, from US corn to cosmetics and Chinese toys to household appliances. However there were some notable omissions on each side, including non-seed soybeans, the biggest US agricultural export to China.

articles.title: US visa wait hits 346 days; India staff face load
articles.summary: India’s US consular officers handled an average of 21,401 nonimmigrant visa applications each in fiscal year 2025, the highest workload among major visa-processing countries, according to a US Government Accountability Office report.The staffing pressure has coincided with a sharp increase in interview waits. The weighted average wait to schedule a US nonimmigrant visa interview in India reached 346 days in FY25.The US State Department received 1,455,255 nonimmigrant visa applications in India during the year. Only 68 consular officers were working on nonimmigrant visas.By comparison, China had 119 officers handling 1.2 million applications, or 10,135 applications per officer. Brazil had 87 officers handling 1.14 million applications, while Mexico had 124 officers handling 2.66 million applications.India also recorded the longest interview wait among the four countries examined by the GAO. The average wait was 283 days in Mexico, 34 days in China and 32 days in Brazil.The wait for a visitor visa interview in India increased from 42 days in FY19 to 346 days in FY25. The GAO said the wait in India and Mexico was more than eight times longer than before the Covid-19 pandemic.US consular officials told the GAO that inadequate staffing compared with demand was a major factor behind the long waits. Lower staffing levels limited the number of interviews that posts could conduct and contributed to backlogs.The number of officers working on nonimmigrant visas worldwide fell from 1,342 in FY24 to 904 in FY25. State Department officials attributed the decline to a hiring freeze, a reduction in force and attrition.The department sent more than 100 consular officers and locally employed staff on temporary assignments to countries including India and Mexico in FY23. However, the GAO said high demand continued to keep interview waits elevated.The State Department also did not complete its global staffing exercise in FY24 and FY25. The exercise is meant to assess workloads and determine whether staff should be moved between posts.The GAO recommended that the department establish a policy requiring it to conduct the exercise consistently.The 346-day figure refers to the time taken to secure a visa interview. It does not represent the time taken to receive a final visa decision.
